newsitem.title: UK: EU gas directive could be adopted by Dec - official.
newsitem.headline: EU gas directive could be adopted by Dec - official.

text.p: The European Union's natural gas directive could be law by the end of this year if a common position is reached under the Dutch EU presidency in May, a Commission official said on Monday.

Francesco Meggiolaro of the Energy Department of the European Commission told an SMi gas industry conference that assuming a common position is reached in May, the gas directive could follow the same timetable as the electricity directive, adopted into law in December last year.

It could be approved by the European parliament in December and adopted the same month, after which national legislatures in each member state would have two years to ratify it. At the most optimistic estimate, Meggiolaro said, it could have the force of law in each member state by December 1999.
He added that market liberalisation in "networked" energy industries - gas and electricity, as opposed to the "non-networked" industries of oil and coal - has only been achieved in a few countries.
Britain has liberalised or partly liberalised both electricity and gas markets, while Sweden and Finland have done so in electricity only and Spain has recently started in gas only.

Progress is also underway n Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Ireland and Portugal, he added, with some legislation presented or discussions under way. In all other member states, "no real steps have been taken", he said.

The main proposals under discussion concern public service obligations which gas suppliers will have to customers in a liberalised market; access to pipeline networks; "unbundling", or separation of services currently provided by large gas companies and monopolies, as well as increasing transparency of accounting systems; and specific reference to long term "take or pay" contracts.

Meggiolaro said that the EU recognised that take or pay contracts, under which buyers undertake to pay for gas supplies over the length of the contract regardless of whether or not they choose to take them, are specific to the gas sector. He also said EU was aware of problems which could arise from opening the market too quickly.

After the restart of gas directive negotiations in July last year, there were several months of industry consultations before the Irish Presidency of the EU published a compromise text taking into account the years of development in the industry since the proposals were initiated.

This was judged to be a good basis for further debate, said Meggiolaro, and provided hope that a common position could be reached during the Dutch presidency in May, leading to the possibility of adoption by the end of the year.
